page_title: Algorithms for scalable synchronization on shared-memory multiprocessors

sources.entry: Algorithms for Scalable Synchronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors - The origin of the queue lock, each waiter spinning on its own line, measured against ticket and test-and-set locks.

summary.title: Algorithms for Scalable Synchronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors
summary.one_liner: Mellor-Crummey and Scott's 1991 paper shows how to build spin locks and barriers that spin only on locally accessible flags, eliminating busy-wait memory and interconnect contention, and compares them on Sequent Symmetry and BBN Butterfly machines.
keywords: how to avoid lock contention on multiprocessors
takeaways: Busy-wait contention comes from many processors polling one shared location; spinning on separate locally accessible flags avoids it.
Test-and-set locks with exponential backoff and ticket locks with proportional backoff reduce polling traffic but still contend on a shared location.
Array-based queuing locks let each waiter spin on its own cache line, giving constant remote references per acquisition using only fetch-and-increment or fetch-and-store.
The paper also presents a scalable barrier needing O(1) remote references per processor and argues that software can rival special-purpose synchronization hardware.
summary.summary: The paper surveys busy-wait spin locks (test-and-set with backoff, ticket lock, Anderson's and Graunke-Thakkar's array-based queuing locks) and explains how each reduces memory and interconnect contention. It introduces a new scalable spin lock with O(1) remote references per acquisition that needs only a swap-with-memory instruction, and a new barrier with O(1) remote references per processor. Performance is measured on a Sequent Symmetry and a BBN Butterfly, with pseudo-code for each algorithm. The authors conclude that software synchronization can scale and that this weakens the case for costly hardware support and for dance-hall memory architectures.
